overlap_rationale: The PDF supplied for Study B (cited as Bradshaw & Huby 2013, Journal of Poverty and Social Justice 21(2):137-148, DOI 10.1332/175982713X669835) is a mismatched duplicate file identical byte-for-byte (SHA-256: 716a147031228c06b4ea094ff44085333f1df3889d94dbe4f4b47b61632ddcba) to Study A (Sylvester, Hutchings & Mdee 2023, Water Policy 25(5):492-511, DOI 10.2166/wp.2023.253). Because Study B's actual full text is missing/mismatched, mandatory audit rules require setting pair_classification to cannot_tell_missing_full_text, same_underlying_data to cannot_tell, and synthesis_double_counting_risk to cannot_tell. What can be verified from Study A's text alone is that Study A is a 2023 systematic-style literature review of 354 academic and grey documents (1985-2022) on water poverty in England and Wales that explicitly cites and summarises Bradshaw & Huby (2013) (reporting 2009/10 Family Resources Survey water poverty prevalence of 23.6% at the 3% threshold and 11.5% at the 5% threshold, and mean water poverty gaps of £3.46 and £3.62). However, without the authentic full text of Bradshaw & Huby (2013), Study B's exact sample size, analytical specifications, and primary empirical tables cannot be directly verified, and the retrieval error in the corpus would cause Study A's text to be read twice if uncorrected.
study_a_sample_and_data: Systematic-style narrative literature review of N = 354 grey and academic documents published between 1985 and 2022 (searched across 4 academic and 35 grey databases using the SPIDER framework and coded in NVivo) examining household water poverty, affordability (3% and 5% disposable income thresholds), customer vulnerability, and utility bad debt in England and Wales. Secondary summary tables compile historical estimates from prior studies, including Bradshaw & Huby (2013).
study_b_sample_and_data: True full text not accessible due to a PDF retrieval mismatch: the file provided under Study B (SHA-256: 716a147031228c06b4ea094ff44085333f1df3889d94dbe4f4b47b61632ddcba) is another copy of Sylvester, Hutchings & Mdee (2023), DOI 10.2166/wp.2023.253, rather than Bradshaw & Huby (2013), DOI 10.1332/175982713X669835. Second-hand citations within Study A indicate Bradshaw & Huby (2013) analysed 2009/10 Department for Work and Pensions Family Resources Survey data for England and Wales, but Study B's primary sample size, methods, and results cannot be verified directly.
